stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a 2019 field study of a coastal dialect, researchers recorded three features that set local speech apart from the regional standard: the dropping of final consonants, as in "han" for "hand"; a merger of vowels in words such as "pin" and "pen," which most speakers pronounce identically______ a habitual "be," used to mark actions that happen repeatedly.
explanation: This sentence lists three features, and the items already contain commas ("pin" and "pen," which...). The first and second items are already separated by a semicolon after "hand." To match that pattern, you also need a semicolon before the final item, so "identically; and" is correct.

A.why: You chose the comma because of the words right around the blank. The list already uses a semicolon between its first two items, though, and the items contain their own commas. A comma here makes it unclear where the second item stops.

C.why: You put a colon in the middle of a list. A colon can introduce a list, and this sentence already has one before "the dropping." A second colon between list items doesn't tell the reader that a new item is starting.

D.why: You ended the sentence early. The words after the period ("And a habitual 'be,' used to mark actions...") have no main verb, so they form a fragment and not a complete sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A recent recital series set out to recover music by women composers whom concert programs had long overlooked. Its opening evening featured three figures from different centuries: Hildegard of Bingen, a twelfth-century abbess and visionary______ Barbara Strozzi, a Venetian singer who published eight volumes of her own songs; and Fanny Mendelssohn, several of whose early works first appeared under her brother's name.
explanation: Each composer's name is followed by a descriptive phrase that contains its own comma, and the later items are separated by a semicolon ("songs; and Fanny"). The separator at the blank has to match that, so you need a semicolon after "visionary."

B.why: You fell for the subtype's trap. After "Hildegard of Bingen," a comma looks natural, but the rest of the list uses semicolons. With a comma here, Barbara Strozzi could be read as another description of Hildegard instead of a separate composer.

C.why: You used a colon between two list items. A colon here would make Strozzi look like an explanation of Hildegard's description, and the sentence already has a colon that introduces the list.

D.why: You chose a single dash. A single dash works like a colon, so it would make the rest of the list an explanation of "visionary." It also doesn't match the semicolons that separate the other items.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before synthetic dyes arrived in the 1850s, European cloth dyers worked with a small range of plant sources. Most workshops kept three on hand: madder, whose roots yield a deep, durable red; weld, a flowering herb that produces a bright yellow______ woad, which gives a blue that darkens as the cloth is exposed to air.
explanation: The first two items are separated by a semicolon ("red; weld"), and the first item contains a comma of its own ("deep, durable"). The final item needs the same separator, so the correct choice is "yellow; and."

A.why: You decided from the nearby words, where the internal commas make a comma look fine. You didn't check the rest of the list, which already uses a semicolon after "red." The separators in a list have to match.

B.why: With no punctuation, the sentence seems to say that weld produces both yellow and woad. Nothing marks where the second item ends, and the list's semicolon pattern is dropped.

C.why: You placed a colon inside the list. A colon introduces what follows it, and this list is already introduced after "on hand." A colon between the second and third items doesn't make sense grammatically.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Portolan charts, the nautical maps that first appeared in Genoa and Venice around 1270, look strikingly different from other medieval maps. Historians point to three traits: rhumb lines, which radiate from compass roses across the open sea______ coastlines traced with surprising accuracy, particularly around the Mediterranean; and an almost complete lack of inland detail.
explanation: Look past the blank. The second and third traits are separated by a semicolon ("Mediterranean; and"), and the items contain commas and "which" clauses. The first and second traits need a matching semicolon, so "sea;" is correct.

A.why: You chose a comma because the item before the blank ends with a "which" clause that a comma could easily continue. The rest of the list uses a semicolon, though, and a comma here mixes the two separators.

B.why: You treated the list as a series of sentences. "Coastlines traced with surprising accuracy...and an almost complete lack of inland detail" has no main verb, so the period leaves a fragment.

D.why: You used a colon between two items in a list. That would make the coastlines an explanation of the rhumb lines, and the list already has a colon after "three traits."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Infrared telescopes can detect faint objects that give off almost no visible light. One planned survey will catalog three such categories: brown dwarfs, which are too small to sustain hydrogen fusion______ rogue planets, which drift through the galaxy without a host star; and white dwarfs, the dense, cooling remnants of stars like the Sun.
explanation: Each category is followed by a descriptive phrase, some with internal commas ("dense, cooling"). The later items are separated by a semicolon ("star; and white dwarfs"). To match, you need a semicolon between the first and second items: "fusion;".

A.why: You fell for the trap. A comma after a "which" clause sounds natural, but the list already uses a semicolon after "star." When the items contain commas, a comma separator makes it unclear where one item ends and the next begins.

C.why: You added "and" with no punctuation. Then the sentence seems to say that brown dwarfs are too small to sustain both fusion and rogue planets. It also uses "and" in the middle of a list and again before the final item.

D.why: You opened a dash, which works like a colon. It would make rogue planets an explanation of brown dwarfs, and it doesn't match the semicolons that separate the other items.
